subject: history_social
passage: At the end of a meal in a Chinese restaurant in the United States, diners are usually given fortune cookies: crisp, folded cookies with a slip of paper inside that carries a short message. Because the cookies are served in Chinese restaurants, many diners assume they are an old Chinese tradition.
passage_b: Fortune cookies were being made by Japanese bakers in California in the early 1900s, based on a folded cracker from Kyoto that also carried a paper message. Chinese restaurants in the United States adopted the cookies later, and they spread across the country after World War II. In China itself, fortune cookies were almost unknown until recent decades.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that fortune cookies were first made in Kyoto by Chinese cooks
choices.B: By explaining that the cookie began with Japanese bakers in the United States
choices.C: By arguing that Chinese restaurants should stop serving fortune cookies
choices.D: By agreeing that fortune cookies have been eaten in China for centuries

explanation.why: Text 1 says diners assume fortune cookies are "an old Chinese tradition." Text 2 traces them instead to "Japanese bakers in California in the early 1900s" and notes that in China they "were almost unknown until recent decades." So the author of Text 2 would correct the assumption with this history.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the Kyoto cracker was Japanese and that the cookies were made in California, not in Kyoto by Chinese cooks.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 says the cookies started with Japanese bakers in California and were adopted by Chinese restaurants later.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 gives a history; it does not tell restaurants what to serve.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the cookies were almost unknown in China until recently, so its author would not agree.
